questions.q: Why couldn't a self-custodial protocol freeze a user's wallet the way a centralized exchange froze withdrawals during the FTX collapse?
options: Self-custodial protocols always have a government guarantee against freezes
There's no account or company in the loop — the user's wallet holds the asset directly, not a company-controlled balance
Self-custodial protocols are required by law to never pause anything
Centralized exchanges and DeFi protocols work identically under the hood
questions.explain: FTX could freeze withdrawals because it held custody of user assets. A self-custodial protocol has no custody to revoke in the first place.

questions.q: What distinguishes a "Read" function from a "Write" function on a verified contract?
options: Read functions report state with no gas cost and no signature; Write functions change state and require a signed, gas-paying transaction
Read functions cost gas and Write functions are free
Read functions can only be called by the contract's admin
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: getReserves() or balanceOf() just report current state for free; swap() or mint() actually change state and require you to sign and pay gas.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between USDC and DAI as stablecoins?
options: USDC and DAI use the exact same collateral model
DAI is backed by fiat reserves and USDC is backed by crypto
USDC is fiat-collateralized by real-world dollar reserves; DAI is crypto-collateralized by an overcollateralized basket of on-chain assets
Neither stablecoin uses any form of collateral
questions.explain: USDC's value is backed by real dollars held in reserve off-chain; DAI's value comes from crypto collateral locked on-chain, held above the debt it backs.

questions.q: Why does a 50 ETH trade move the price far more (in percentage terms) than a 1 ETH trade in the same pool?
options: Because larger trades are charged a higher percentage fee by the protocol
Because the pool resets its reserves between large trades
There is no actual difference in price impact between trade sizes
Because the x*y=k curve is a hyperbola that steepens as a reserve is depleted, so larger trades face disproportionately worse pricing
questions.explain: The worked table shows price impact growing from about -1% at 1 ETH to over -33% at 50 ETH — a direct result of the curve's shape, not a fee schedule.

questions.q: What is the main inefficiency of full-range liquidity (the model from Lessons 5-8)?
options: Most of an LP's capital sits at price levels that will realistically never be reached, earning zero fees while still deployed
It charges LPs a higher trading fee than concentrated pools
It cannot accept deposits from more than one LP at a time
It requires LPs to actively manage their position every day
questions.explain: Full-range liquidity spreads capital across the entire 0-to-infinity price curve, even though a pair usually trades in a narrow band, leaving most capital idle.

questions.q: Impermanent loss is the gap between an LP position's value and what?
options: The value of the pool's LP token at its all-time high
The protocol's total trading fee revenue for the day
What the LP would have if they had simply held the two assets separately instead of depositing them
The value of a completely unrelated, uncorrelated asset
questions.explain: IL is specifically defined relative to the "HODL alternative" — simply holding the deposited assets rather than providing liquidity with them.

questions.q: What does an aToken represent when you deposit into a lending pool?
options: A governance vote with no connection to your deposit
An interest-bearing receipt token representing your deposit, redeemable 1:1 for the underlying asset plus accrued interest
A fixed-price voucher unrelated to interest
A penalty charged for depositing collateral
questions.explain: An aToken's balance grows as interest accrues to suppliers, and it's redeemed 1:1 for the underlying asset plus that accrued interest on withdrawal.

questions.q: Why is the supply rate always lower than the borrow rate in the same pool?
options: Because supply rates and borrow rates are actually always identical
Because suppliers are charged an extra fee on top of the borrow rate
Because suppliers only earn a share of interest scaled by utilization, and the protocol also takes a reserve factor cut
Because only borrowers are allowed to earn any interest at all
questions.explain: Only the utilized portion of the pool generates interest, and the reserve factor is held back before interest reaches suppliers, so the supply rate is always below the borrow rate.

questions.q: What formula does the healthFactor() function implement?
options: collateral value divided by total supply
(collateral value * liquidation threshold) / debt — the same formula from Lesson 10
A random number generated per block
debt divided by collateral value, with no threshold applied
questions.explain: healthFactor() computes (collateral[user] * getPrice() * 8000 / 10000) / debt[user], exactly Lesson 10's (collateral value * liquidation threshold) / borrowed value.

questions.q: A farm emits $2,000,000/year in reward value into a pool with $10,000,000 TVL. What is the farm APY by this lesson's formula?
questions.explain: farm_APY = (annual_reward_value_USD / TVL_USD) x 100 = (2,000,000 / 10,000,000) x 100 = 20%.

questions.q: What is a performance fee, as distinct from a management fee?
options: A fixed annual fee on total assets regardless of performance
A one-time fee charged only at deposit
A fee that only applies if the vault loses money
A percentage taken only from actual profit the strategy generates, not from principal
questions.explain: A performance fee (commonly 10-20%) is charged only on gains; a management fee (commonly 0-2%) is charged on assets regardless of performance.

questions.q: Under the halving example (initial rate 50 tokens/block, halving every 210,000 blocks), what is the reward rate for blocks 210,001-420,000?
options: 50 tokens/block
12.5 tokens/block
0 tokens/block
25 tokens/block
questions.explain: After the first halving interval, the rate drops to half of 50, which is 25 tokens/block.

questions.q: Why does a cliff specifically help prevent early dumping, beyond what a long vesting duration alone would do?
options: A cliff has no additional effect beyond vesting duration
Cliffs only apply to governance tokens, not utility tokens
A cliff guarantees the token price will rise
Without a cliff, insiders could sell immediately after the token generation event, directly into launch-day demand
questions.explain: The cliff specifically blocks any unlocking in the earliest period, which is when insiders would otherwise be able to sell straight into the demand a launch creates.

questions.q: Why can a market cap calculated from total supply (instead of circulating supply) be misleading?
options: It overstates how much of the token is actually liquid and tradeable right now
Total supply is always smaller than circulating supply
It has no effect -- the two numbers are always identical
Total supply excludes locked tokens, so it understates market cap
questions.explain: Total supply includes locked, vesting, and treasury-held tokens that aren't actually on the market, so using it inflates the apparent market cap.

questions.q: In the worked comparison, why is Protocol A's 150% APY considered fragile?
options: 150% APY is always a fraud regardless of its source
It is backed entirely by real trading fee revenue
It's backed almost entirely by $15,000,000 in new token issuance against only $50,000 in real revenue
The protocol has no emissions at all
questions.explain: The yield only holds its value as long as the token price survives the weight of $15,000,000/year in new supply -- it's not backed by real revenue.

questions.q: In the default 1-token-1-vote model shown in this lesson's Tally screenshot, what determines a voter's power?
options: The number of tokens they hold plus whatever's been delegated to them
The number of proposals they've previously voted on
A fixed amount, identical for every address
How long ago they joined the protocol
questions.explain: voting_power(address) = balance(address) + sum(delegated_to(address)) -- the default model this lesson describes.

questions.q: Per Compound's own published governance lifecycle diagram shown in this lesson, what stage comes immediately after a proposal succeeds and before it executes?
options: Immediate execution with no delay
A second, separate vote
Queued in the Timelock (a delay period)
Automatic cancellation
questions.explain: Compound's diagram shows Succeeded -> Queued (Timelock, 2 days) -> Executed -- a delay sits between a vote passing and the change actually applying.

questions.q: Which two checks does execute() perform that directly implement Lesson 24's quorum and majority rules?
options: require(block.timestamp > p.voteEnd, ...) and require(!p.executed, ...) only
There are no quorum or majority checks in execute()
require(totalVotes >= QUORUM, ...) and require(p.forVotes > p.againstVotes, ...)
A single require statement checks both at once with no separate logic
questions.explain: The quorum check verifies total participation meets QUORUM; the majority check verifies forVotes exceeds againstVotes -- both must pass for execution to proceed.

questions.q: Per this lesson's guidance, which project would best fit ERC-1155 rather than ERC-721?
options: A game that needs gold, swords, shields, and other item types all managed efficiently in one contract
A single 1-of-1 piece of generative art with unique provenance
A deed representing ownership of one unique real-world property
A collection where every token must be completely unique with no shared type
questions.explain: ERC-1155 fits well when a project needs many token types (fungible, semi-fungible, or unique) managed together and often transferred/minted in batches, like game items.

questions.q: Why do NFT-backed lending protocols typically use a lower loan-to-value ratio than fungible-asset lending protocols, per this lesson?
options: NFTs are always worth more than fungible tokens
A single NFT's value depends on floor price estimates, rarity traits, and thin order books -- harder to price than a liquid fungible token
Regulations ban NFT-backed loans from using high LTV
There is no real difference -- both use identical LTV ratios
questions.explain: Pricing a specific, illiquid NFT is harder than pricing a continuously-traded fungible asset, so protocols compensate with a lower LTV.

questions.q: What does the real ERC-2981 royaltyInfo(tokenId, salePrice) function return?
options: The current owner of the token only
A boolean indicating whether the sale is allowed
The full list of all past owners
The receiver address and the royalty amount owed for that sale price
questions.explain: royaltyInfo returns (address receiver, uint256 royaltyAmount) -- who should be paid and how much, for a given sale price.
